As you can surmise from the above comparisons, You Got Older is a complex layered piece that is told in a refreshingly simple way that will make you laugh at life’s absurdities and perhaps shed a tear at its soft touches.
Rarely has a play made me feel more seen.
You Got Older remains a timeless meditation on adulthood in all its messiness, pain, and sometimes humor — and it is well worth seeing.
If you can stomach some of the other references here, Mr. Friedman’s presence makes this staging of “You Got Older” worth catching.
What’s missing is an evident sense of anger or resentment, or much more than a nod to anxiety and sorrow.
You Got Older is a messy, moving portrait of a family in freefall.
You Got Older nails the complicated dynamics of families, and how patterns of behavior can calcify as well as evolve over time.

Anne Kauffman's production, hampered by Barron's fundamentally underwritten script, offers neither intimacy nor its meaningful absence—just a sluggish 105 minutes with people we never quite come to know.
Both their plays are bearing testament to the existence of functional families—onstage and off—and the power of that unconditional love.

cn.t: Barron's intimate family drama about a millennial caring for her cancer-stricken father earns praise for its tender honesty and dark humor, though some find its banal chatter and quiet scenes overly understated.

vr.q: I'd argue that the understated nature here is what makes it so resonant and impactful in a way that reminded me of the film Lady Bird.
